headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; Windsurf’s MCP/clipboard/file surfaces plus AutoGen’s writable execution environment create unsafe default interaction paths.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Windsurf can ingest clipboard, workspace files, and MCP content, while AutoGen can write files and execute shell commands in shared working directories. That creates a realistic path for attacker-controlled content from one agent to be treated as instructions by the other. The pair’s interaction is not documented as provenance-safe, so uncertainty pushes upward.
conditions: IF both agents share a writable workspace or clipboard bridge, injected instructions can cross from one agent to the other.
IF Windsurf reads AutoGen-produced files as trusted task text, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct directories.
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents.
Require human review of any file passed from AutoGen to Windsurf.
Turn off MCP connections unless explicitly needed.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging and instruction/content separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen reads and writes files in configured working directories, and Windsurf shares state via the local filesystem while also handling open files and workspace files. If sensitive application data is present in that shared workspace, either agent can expose it through model-provider or MCP/API calls. The profiles do not show isolation by default, so leakage risk is substantial.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared workspace, both agents can read them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to its backend or model proxy, those contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Move sensitive files out of the shared workspace.
Use separate OS users or containers for each agent.
Restrict both agents to least-privilege directories.
Review and disable unnecessary model-proxy or API integrations.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls and redaction.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and run shell commands, and Windsurf additionally modifies git state while AutoGen can spawn subprocesses and install packages. In a shared directory, concurrent edits and git operations can collide, causing lost work or corrupted state. Because no locking is documented, the safer choice is high rather than medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository or directory, file-write conflicts can occur.
IF Windsurf auto-executes terminal actions while AutoGen is also mutating files, state corruption becomes plausible.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree.
Pause one agent before the other edits shared files.
Avoid concurrent git operations in the same repo.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen can generate code, plans, and file outputs that Windsurf may then consume in its editor workflow. Windsurf’s agentic loop can act on those inputs, so unverified AutoGen output can cascade into downstream edits or commands. This is not proven to be fully automatic, but the default interaction path is plausible enough for medium severity.
conditions: IF Windsurf treats AutoGen-produced text as authoritative task context, errors can propagate.
IF AutoGen emits incorrect code or instructions that Windsurf applies without verification, downstream mistakes multiply.
mitigations: Require explicit verification before Windsurf acts on AutoGen output.
Insert a human review step for generated code or plans.
Limit AutoGen to draft-only outputs.
Use tests or linting before applying changes.
requires-engineering: build a validation gate between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen is open-source and configurable, while Windsurf is closed-source and routes calls through a model proxy and optional MCP servers. If regulated data such as source code secrets or personal data is processed in the shared workspace, retention and residency behavior may differ across the pair. The profiles do not document aligned compliance controls, so mismatch risk is medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed through Windsurf’s model proxy or MCP servers, external retention/residency obligations may apply.
IF the same sensitive workspace is used under both agents, differing logging or retention policies can create a compliance gap.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Review vendor retention and residency settings before use.
Disable optional MCP integrations for regulated projects.
Document which data classes each agent may process.
requires-engineering: obtain and enforce a DPA or equivalent controls.
